title: Washington, Mason County
summary: Washington in Mason County grew from about 700 acres that Arthur Fox and Baptist preacher William Wood laid out as a one-mile-square town in 1785.
bodyMarkdown:
Washington, in Mason County, is one of the oldest towns in Kentucky and one of the earliest American settlements west of the Appalachians. Today it is a neighborhood of Maysville, a few miles inland from the Ohio River. In its first decades it was among the busiest places on the Kentucky frontier.

## Founding

[The Washington Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Historic_District_(Washington,_Kentucky)) traces settlement to May 1775. A party of ten men came from farther east in Virginia to survey and improve land, and one of them, Jonathan Higgs, built a cabin. Simon Kenton cleared land nearby.

In 1785 Kenton sold 700 acres to two Virginians, Arthur Fox and William Wood, who laid out a one-mile-square grid and sold lots. [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_Kentucky) says Fox, a Revolutionary War soldier, and Wood, a Baptist preacher, founded the town in 1786, and that Daniel Boone was among its first trustees. The [Grokipedia entry on Maysville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Maysville,_Kentucky) gives a different founder: it says Simon Kenton founded the village in 1786. The town was chartered as Washington, Virginia, since Kentucky was not yet a state.

## A frontier hub

The 1790 census counted 462 residents, including 21 enslaved people. Only Lexington was larger. The historic district article records 119 houses that year. Washington became the Mason County seat in 1788, and a courthouse followed in 1794.

In 1789 the town's post office became a mail center for the region north of the Ohio, but the two Wikipedia articles list the states differently. The Washington article names Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin and Minnesota. The historic district article names Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin.

## Slavery and the Civil War

Washington's history includes slavery. Thornton Blackburn was enslaved in a local house from 1815 to 1824, and later escaped to Canada. His case helped confirm Canada as a refuge for freedom seekers.

In 1833 the young teacher Harriet Beecher, later Harriet Beecher Stowe, visited and saw a slave auction. One account places it in front of the old courthouse, while another places it at the Paxton Inn. Both say the experience shaped Uncle Tom's Cabin.

The town produced generals on both sides. Confederate Albert Sidney Johnston was born there in 1803. Union general William "Bull" Nelson grew up in the same house.

## Decline

Washington lost ground to Maysville, the river town. Fire in 1825 and cholera in 1832–33 hurt the town. The two Wikipedia articles date the loss of the county seat differently: the Washington article says 1848, while the historic district article says 1847. The road to Lexington later drew national attention in [the Maysville Road veto of 1830](/stories/the-maysville-road-and-jacksons-veto-1830/).

## Kentucky today

The Washington Historic District was listed on the National Register in 1970 and enlarged in 1976. Maysville annexed Washington in 1990. Many log buildings survive, and the town keeps several museums, including the Albert Sidney Johnston/Bull Nelson House.
